title: Try a Short Breath Meditation
description: Sit somewhere safe, let your breathing stay natural, notice when attention wanders, and bring it back. If starting is the hard part, you can attach the practice to a stable daily routine. The cue is an implementation option, not a proven adherence hack, and five minutes is still a convenient container rather than a therapeutic dose.

trusted_protocol.title: Try a Short Breath Meditation
trusted_protocol.description: Sit somewhere safe, let your breathing stay natural, notice when attention wanders, and bring it back. If starting is the hard part, you can attach the practice to a stable daily routine. The cue is an implementation option, not a proven adherence hack, and five minutes is still a convenient container rather than a therapeutic dose.
trusted_protocol.action: Sit somewhere comfortable and safe. Let breathing stay natural. Notice the sensations of breathing; when attention drifts into plans, memories, sounds or commentary, notice that and return to the breath without grading yourself. Use five minutes only if it is a convenient starting container. If initiation is the problem, choose one recurring non-safety-critical cue — for example after closing the laptop for lunch or after finishing your evening hygiene — and let that cue mean 'try the short practice now.' After several attempts, keep the cue only if it reduces friction without making the practice annoying or compulsory.
trusted_protocol.check_in: Did I notice attention wandering and return without turning it into a fight? If I used a routine cue, did it actually make starting easier? Was the practice useful, neutral or uncomfortable? Would another wellbeing practice fit me better today?
